definition.text: The strip where land meets a river or stream, with its own water-loving vegetation.

facts.text: The name comes from the Latin ripa, meaning river bank; such strips are also called riparian buffer zones, corridors or strips.
Riparian zones act as natural biofilters, shielding waters from too much sediment, polluted runoff and erosion.
They give shelter and food to many aquatic animals, and their shade limits changes in stream temperature.
Buffer zones can cut nitrate pollution from manure and fertilizer washing off farm fields, and wetland riparian zones remove nitrate especially well.
Land beside a watercourse that stays waterlogged for a season or more is usually called a wetland instead, because of its hydric soils.
Because they support so many species, riparian zones are often protected under national biodiversity action plans.
Riparian zones may be natural, or engineered to stabilize soil or restore damaged land.

definition.text: The benefits riparian zones provide, from slowing floods and filtering runoff to wildlife habitat and recreation.

facts.text: River bends, plants and roots slow the water, which reduces soil erosion and flood damage, while trapped sediment leaves water clearer and builds banks.
They serve as wildlife corridors, letting aquatic and riparian organisms move along rivers instead of living in isolated groups.
Thinning riparian vegetation brings higher and more variable stream temperatures, and extreme temperature swings can kill fish.
Riparian zones raise nearby property values through views and amenity, and create space for fishing, swimming and boating.

definition.text: Leaving riparian strips undisturbed during timber harvesting so they keep protecting the stream.

facts.text: Undisturbed soil and vegetation along the stream give shade, leaf litter and wood, and hold back soil eroded from the logged area.
How well a buffer works depends on soil type, root structure, climate and plant cover.
Logging degrades riparian zones through added sediment, introduced or removed species and polluted water.

definition.text: Repairing damaged riverbanks through removing human structures, active rehabilitation, or simply giving them time.

facts.text: Clearing land and then flooding can quickly strip a riverbank of grasses and soil.
Methods range from erosion control and replanting to log sills, pin groynes and rock placement, invasive species control, and leaving areas alone to regrow.
Fast-growing pioneer 'weeds' can be used to kick-start succession, stabilizing soil until trees and grasses return.
Conservationists urge that the value of riparian ecosystem services be written into management plans, where it has usually been left out.

definition.text: An underwater ecosystem made up of seagrasses, flowering plants that grow in shallow coastal and estuary waters.

facts.text: Seagrass meadows rank among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, supporting marine life as diverse as coral reefs do.
Seagrasses descend from land plants that returned to the sea about 75 to 100 million years ago.
They grow on the continental shelves of every continent except Antarctica, down to depths of about 60 metres.
They prefer sheltered bays, lagoons and estuaries where waves are small and light and nutrients plentiful.
They shelter endangered species such as seahorses, turtles and dugongs, and are nurseries for shrimps, scallops and many commercial fish.
Pollution from land runoff, dredges and trawls, and overfishing are damaging meadows, which are being destroyed at about 3 square metres per second.

definition.text: The goods and services seagrass meadows give coastal areas, such as cleaner water, oxygen, food and shelter.

facts.text: Seagrasses improve water quality by locking up heavy metals and other toxins, removing excess nutrients and lowering acidity.
They release large amounts of oxygen into the water, and their roots oxygenate the sediment for the animals living in it.
Turtles, parrotfish, surgeonfish and sea urchins eat the grass, while small invertebrates feed on films on the leaves.
Conserving seagrass meadows supports 16 of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Near small Indonesian islands without sewage treatment, harmful bacteria such as Enterococcus were 50 percent lower where seagrass was present.
Seagrass was once gathered as fertilizer for sandy soils and used to stuff mattresses.

definition.text: The carbon dioxide seagrass meadows pull from the air and bury in seabed sediment, part of coastal blue carbon.

facts.text: Seagrass meadows cover only 0.1% of the ocean floor yet account for 10–18% of all carbon buried in the ocean.
Per hectare they hold twice as much carbon dioxide as rain forests and can sequester about 27 million tons of CO2 a year.
Global seagrass meadows are estimated to store up to 19.9 Pg (billion tons) of organic carbon.
Carbon builds up in low-oxygen seabed sediments, where slow decomposition preserves it for decades to millennia.
Unlike land habitats that lose carbon to decay, fire or deforestation, marine sinks can keep carbon far longer.
Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 140 g C m−2 yr−1.
Restored seagrass meadows began storing carbon in sediment within about four years.

conflicts.text: The Blue carbon article gives the average seagrass carbon burial rate as approximately 138 g C m−2 yr−1.
conflicts.note: Seagrass meadow gives about 140 g C m−2 yr−1 for the same average; likely a rounding of the same figure.

definition.text: How seagrass leaves and roots calm waves and hold sediment, protecting coasts from erosion and storm surge.

facts.text: Seagrasses are ecosystem engineers that reshape their surroundings physically and chemically.
Leaves slow currents so sediment settles and builds up the seafloor; without seagrass, currents carry it away and erode the bottom.
By reducing wave energy and building sediment they protect houses and cities from the sea and from sea-level rise.

definition.text: The role of seagrass meadows as sheltered nurseries for young fish and shellfish that later support fisheries.

facts.text: About half of global fisheries are estimated to get their start in seagrass habitats; lose the seagrass and the fisheries go too.
Seagrass gives nursery habitat to over 1/5th of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species.
A 2019 study found this role is poorly reflected in the decisions of the authorities who manage seagrass.
Gleaning for shellfish in intertidal seagrass feeds hundreds of millions of people, and small-scale seagrass fisheries act as a safety net for the poor.

definition.text: The worldwide loss of seagrass meadows, driven mostly by human activity.

facts.text: Some 30,000 km2 (12,000 sq mi) of seagrass has been lost in recent decades.
Loss sped up from 0.9% per year before 1940 to 7% per year in 1990.
Bottom-dragged fishing nets and boat propellers physically destroy meadows.
Excess nitrogen and phosphorus feed algae that smother seagrass and block light, starting a feedback loop that can replace seagrass with algae.
Overfishing top predators may boost algae indirectly through a trophic cascade that reduces small grazers.
Low-oxygen water starves seagrass roots and can kill meadows, and the decay of dead plants then uses up more oxygen.
Warming, sedimentation and coastal development also drive decline, and some models predict Posidonia oceanica will be extinct or nearly so by 2050.
Main protection tools are cutting nutrient and other pollution, marine protected areas, and transplanting.

definition.text: A disease of eelgrass, the most widespread seagrass, caused by the marine slime mold Labyrinthula zosterae.

facts.text: The pathogen enters leaf tissue, impairs photosynthesis and breaks down cells, leaving dark spots and streaks.
Warmer seas fuel outbreaks: after the 2015–2016 northeast Pacific heatwave, prevalence rose from 5–70% in 2013 to 60–90% by 2017.
Over the same period eelgrass shoot density fell by 60%.
Meadows with little disease can mark climate-resilient refuges worth prioritizing for protection and restoration.

definition.text: Re-establishing lost seagrass beds by transplanting plants or sowing seeds and other propagules.

facts.text: Communities in Virginia, Florida, Hawaii and the United Kingdom are restoring beds lost to human activity, and reintroductions improve ecosystem services.
Most restoration has used cuttings, rhizome fragments or cores taken from donor meadows; few projects use seeds.
Seed-based restoration has had low and variable results, with more than 90% of propagules failing to survive.
In Chesapeake Bay several million eelgrass seeds are gathered each year with a mechanical harvester.
